newsitem.title: UK: UK's ITV says Channel 5 hurting BBC2 and C4.
newsitem.headline: UK's ITV says Channel 5 hurting BBC2 and C4.

text.p: Britain's Channel 5 television gained audiences at the expense of terrestrial rivals BBC2 and Channel 4 in its first week of operation, ITV network director Marcus Plantin said on Tuesday.
"BBC1 and ITV appear unaffected by the arrival of Channel 5, while some erosion has been felt by Channel 4 and BBC2," Plantin told reporters as ITV launched its spring/summer schedule.

He said the ITV commercial television network was responding to increased competition by investing 170 million pounds on programming in the coming season, putting the accent on sports, drama and youth.

Plantin said that it was obviously still very early days for Channel 5 but noted that ITV was the only channel to have increased its share of peak-time viewing in the week following the launch of the channel on March 30.

ITV's peak-time share rose to 39.2 percent last week from 38.6 percent in the corresponding period last year. BBC1 had 33.7 percent, down from 34.8 percent a year ago, while Channel 4 dipped from 8.9 percent to 6.7 percent and BBC2 fell from 9.2 percent to 8.4 percent.
Channel 5 claimed a peak-time share of around 3.8 percent in its first week, the remaining eight or so percent of viewing was accounted for by cable and satellite channels.

Advertising-funded Channel 5, in which British media companies Pearson Plc and United News & Media Plc are major shareholders, is aiming for a mainstream audience and is seen as a direct competitor to ITV.
Channel 4 also carries advertisements but has a specific remit to cater for minority tastes, while the two BBC channels are funded by the annual licence fee levy.
However, Channel 5's budget is a fraction of ITV's and the new channel is aiming for an audience share of around five percent by the end of the year.
The new ITV schedule is designed in part to appeal to the young audience which Channel 5 is targeting.
"We've invested more money and we've reduced the number of repeats by a third - from 90 hours to 60 hours this year," Plantin said.
"There's more sport than ever before, more first run drama and more programming tailored for younger audiences."
Plantin said ITV's capture of Formula One motor racing from the BBC in a five-year deal costing an estimated 70 million pounds was already paying off with big audiences.
He said ITV's summer sports offering would also include highlights from matches in the "Tournoi de France", a four-nation soccer tournament featuring England, France, Brazil and Italy.
Other audience-pullers include the launch on terrestrial television of "Millennium", a new U.S. series from Chris Carter, the creator of "The X-Files".
